transcript:
Meeting: Redwood Private (VPC) - security review (audit logs, flow logs, endpoints)
Recorded: 2025-02-11 18:00 UTC
Duration: 52 min
Attendees:
- Colin O'Donnell (Redwood) 
- Kevin Osei (Redwood)
- Bruno Silva (Redwood)
- Priya Nair (Northbridge)
- James Wu (Northbridge)
- Elena Petrova (Northbridge)
- Samir Khan (Northbridge)

---
Summary (auto-generated by Fireflies)
- Discussed audit logging expectations for Redwood Private (VPC), including control plane events, installer logs, and runtime/service logs.
- Reviewed VPC Flow Logs defaults in the alpha Terraform modules and options for CloudWatch vs S3 destinations.
- Clarified private connectivity model (VPC endpoints, DNS/private DNS), and "no public egress" posture.
- Identified action items: Redwood to share Security FAQ + architecture doc + endpoint matrix; customer to confirm retention/KMS/log sink.

Topics
1) Audit logs / evidence for compliance
2) Network logging: VPC Flow Logs and centralized routing
3) Private endpoints: ECR/S3/CloudWatch/STS/etc.
4) Secure defaults: SG rules, no public ingress, optional NAT strategy
5) Next steps / follow-up

Action items
- Redwood (Kevin): Send Security FAQ + logging/audit capabilities doc
- Redwood (Bruno): Share endpoint requirements matrix + example config for private-only endpoints
- Northbridge (James/Elena): Confirm DNS resolver approach and whether private DNS is allowed/required
- Northbridge (Samir): Confirm retention requirements and evidence artifacts needed for GRC

---
Transcript

[00:00] Colin O'Donnell: Alright, I think we're live. Thanks everyone for making time. This is the security review for the Private VPC deployment and the Terraform modules we shared in alpha. Goal today is just to make sure we’re aligned on audit logs, VPC flow logs, and the private connectivity assumptions.

[00:18] Priya Nair: Yep, thanks Colin. We want to understand what logs we get, what we can route to our SIEM, and also what this looks like in a no-public-egress VPC. We have some strict controls.

[00:30] Colin O'Donnell: Perfect. Kevin from our security team is here, and Bruno who’s been implementing the Terraform modules and the “locked down” example.

[00:38] Kevin Osei: Hi everyone.

[00:39] Bruno Silva: Hey.

[00:42] James Wu: Hi.

[00:43] Elena Petrova: Hello.

[00:45] Samir Khan: Hey folks.

[00:47] Colin O'Donnell: Maybe Priya, can you give us the quick version of what your must-haves are? Then we can map to what we do by default and where you’ll need to plug into your existing standards.

[01:00] Priya Nair: Sure. Must-haves: (1) audit trail of admin actions, (2) network telemetry, specifically flow logs, (3) encryption with our own keys where possible, and (4) private connectivity. Ideally no internet at all from the workload. Also we need to be able to demonstrate that model prompts and outputs aren’t leaving our boundary.

[01:21] Colin O'Donnell: Makes sense.

[01:23] Kevin Osei: On the last point, the Private deployment is designed to run inside your VPC. Requests and responses stay in your environment. The only connectivity question is around pulling images/updates and telemetry destinations, which we can do via VPC endpoints and your chosen log sink.

[01:40] Elena Petrova: When you say telemetry, do you mean Redwood sending anything out to you? Or you sending out to Redwood?

[01:47] Colin O'Donnell: Good question. For Private (VPC), you can run it with no outbound to the public internet. The default Terraform pattern assumes VPC endpoints for AWS services (ECR, S3, CloudWatch Logs, STS), and then logs can go to CloudWatch Logs in your account or to S3 in your account. There’s not a requirement to stream logs to Redwood.

[02:07] James Wu: So the control plane is also in our account? Or is there some hosted component that needs to call home?

[02:15] Colin O'Donnell: For this Private VPC mode, the control plane components are deployed in your VPC. Installer orchestrates it. There are optional things like update checks that can be configured, but for your posture, we’d run with private endpoints only and no public egress. Bruno can talk through what the Terraform modules set up.

[02:33] Bruno Silva: Yep. In the alpha modules, there’s a wrapper module we call “redwood-private-vpc” which composes three parts: baseline VPC/subnets/route tables, security groups baseline, and endpoints plus private DNS toggles. Default topology is public, private, isolated subnets — but for “no public egress” customers, we typically don’t even place workloads in public subnets, and NAT can be disabled.

[02:58] Elena Petrova: Sorry, you said public subnets exist by default. That’s going to raise flags.

[03:04] Bruno Silva: Right — to be clear, it’s a baseline module. You can choose the topology. The locked-down example creates no public load balancers and can run with NAT disabled. We still sometimes create a minimal public subnet tier depending on how you want to manage ingress, but it can be omitted. The defaults are secure in terms of security groups; no open inbound.

[03:28] Priya Nair: Our concern is more: if public subnets exist, someone later could place something there.

[03:34] Colin O'Donnell: Totally fair. We can align the example with your standard, and the module supports “existing VPC / existing subnets” adoption too. So you can keep your VPC baseline and just consume subnet IDs. The alpha is meant to reduce variance, not force a public topology.

[03:55] Samir Khan: I’m mostly going to ask about evidence. What do we get for audit logs? Like, if an admin changes config, rotates keys, upgrades versions. Where does that show up?

[04:07] Kevin Osei: Let’s split it:
- AWS-level audit: CloudTrail in your account covers API actions for VPC, endpoints, IAM, etc.
- Platform audit: For the Private control plane, we emit audit events for administrative actions within the Redwood console/control plane (things like config changes, user actions) depending on how you operate it. In Private, those logs are stored in your environment.
- Runtime/service logs: component logs (control plane pods, data plane pods) go to your chosen destination (often CloudWatch Logs).

[04:39] Samir Khan: Is there a separate “audit log” stream vs application logs?

[04:44] Kevin Osei: In the alpha, it’s more of “structured events in logs,” and we recommend routing them separately in your log aggregator using fields. The docs we’ll send calls out recommended retention and the event categories.

[04:58] Priya Nair: What about prompts and outputs, do they show up in logs?

[05:03] Colin O'Donnell: By default, we do not log request payloads. We log metadata like request IDs, timings, model name, error codes. If you enable debug logging, you can get more detail, but we advise against that for production unless you have a scrubber in place.

[05:20] Kevin Osei: Exactly. We treat payload logging as an explicit opt-in. There are controls to avoid inadvertently persisting sensitive text.

[05:30] James Wu: For VPC Flow Logs — what are the defaults? Is it enabled? Where does it go? We route everything to a centralized log archive account.

[05:41] Bruno Silva: The module supports enabling VPC Flow Logs. In the “secure defaults” profile we recommend turning it on. Destination can be CloudWatch Logs or S3. For centralized log account, S3 is often simpler: write to a bucket with a bucket policy allowing the VPC Flow Logs service principal. But CloudWatch cross-account subscription is also possible.

[06:05] Elena Petrova: If it’s CloudWatch, we require CMK encryption and log retention set. Do you set retention?

[06:12] Bruno Silva: We set a default retention in the example (like 30 days) but it’s configurable. Encryption: CloudWatch log group can be encrypted with a KMS key; module has a variable for that.

[06:25] Priya Nair: Good. Also, flow logs aren’t enough. We need application audit and OS-level events sometimes.

[06:32] Colin O'Donnell: Sure. On OS-level events, since this is mostly Kubernetes-based in your VPC, the nodes and cluster audit would be in your environment (EKS audit logs if you use EKS, etc.). The Terraform modules here focus on the VPC foundation; cluster layer is separate.

[06:52] James Wu: Okay. So on private connectivity, can you list the endpoints you require? We’ve been burned by vendors where “private” still meant a lot of exceptions.

[07:02] Bruno Silva: Yeah. At minimum for the installer to pull images and run, we need access to ECR (both the API endpoint and the Docker registry endpoint), S3 (often gateway endpoint for artifact pulls), and CloudWatch Logs if you want logs there. STS is a common gotcha because the nodes or components assume STS for role creds. Depending on your exact configuration, SSM can be optional.

[07:29] Elena Petrova: STS. That’s one we usually block.

[07:33] Kevin Osei: If you’re using IAM roles for service accounts or anything that relies on short-term creds, STS gets involved. In fully locked down, you’d want an interface endpoint for STS and ensure private DNS is enabled for it.

[07:48] Priya Nair: We can do STS endpoint, but we need to understand: is it truly internal to AWS, or is there any public route?

[07:56] James Wu: It’s AWS PrivateLink, it stays on AWS backbone if the endpoint is used. But we need to confirm route tables don’t have 0.0.0.0/0 to IGW for the workload subnets.

[08:07] Bruno Silva: Right, and we can do that. Isolated subnets have no route to IGW or NAT. Private subnets can be configured without NAT as well. And security groups default deny inbound, only allow within the cluster and from the internal load balancer as configured.

[08:28] Elena Petrova: Do you touch NACLs?

[08:31] Bruno Silva: The modules intentionally avoid being opinionated on NACLs in alpha, because most enterprises already have a standard and we don’t want to break things. We document NACL guidance though. Security groups are where we implement least privilege by default.

[08:49] Priya Nair: That’s probably fine. We do NACLs centrally. But we’ll want your recommended ports and flows.

[08:56] Colin O'Donnell: We have that as part of the architecture doc and the endpoint matrix. We’ll send it after the call.

[09:04] Samir Khan: Can we talk retention? For regulated workloads we do 1 year hot searchable, 7 years archive for audit. Does anything in Redwood force a retention cap?

[09:15] Kevin Osei: No. Retention is controlled by your sink: CloudWatch retention or S3 lifecycle policies. We’ll provide recommendations, but you can set it to your standard.

[09:27] Samir Khan: Good.

[09:29] Priya Nair: And encryption. For logs and artifacts, are you able to use customer-managed keys?

[09:35] Bruno Silva: For CloudWatch Logs encryption, yes via KMS key ARN. For S3 flow logs, yes via bucket encryption and CMK. For EBS/EFS etc that’s in the cluster layer, not in this module, but generally yes.

[09:53] Kevin Osei: Also for secrets, we recommend integrating with KMS and your secrets manager pattern. The Terraform modules have “hooks” where you can pass key ARNs; but full secrets orchestration is in the installer/cluster layer.

[10:10] James Wu: On the endpoint policies — do you ship policies that restrict to specific buckets or ECR repos? Or is it open?

[10:19] Bruno Silva: In alpha we provide policy stubs and examples. We don’t hardcode a bucket name because customers differ, but we provide inputs so you can restrict. Same with ECR: you can scope to account or repository.

[10:36] Elena Petrova: We will require that. No broad wildcard.

[10:40] Colin O'Donnell: Understood. In pilot we can help you wire that up.

[10:45] Priya Nair: One more: how do we prove no data exfiltration? Like, what prevents the system from reaching out to the internet?

[10:53] Kevin Osei: The main controls are: (1) routing — no IGW/NAT routes for the subnets that run the workload; (2) VPC endpoints for the AWS dependencies; (3) security group egress scoped to required destinations; and (4) your network monitoring (flow logs). You can also enforce egress at firewall/proxy if you have centralized egress.

[11:18] Elena Petrova: You mentioned SG egress scoped. Are your default SGs allow-all egress? Because many vendors just do 0.0.0.0/0.

[11:28] Bruno Silva: Great point. In the baseline we default to restrictive egress where we can — for example, allow egress only to the endpoints’ security group and within the VPC CIDR. There are some cases where Kubernetes node egress needs to be broader depending on your CNI and cluster add-ons, but for the Redwood components we keep it tight.

[11:54] Priya Nair: Okay. Please document that clearly. Our reviewers will ask.

[11:59] Colin O'Donnell: Will do.

[12:02] James Wu: We’ve looked at AWS Bedrock private link. They have an AWS-managed service endpoint. Your approach is “bring it into our VPC.” That’s better for us but also more work. What’s the operational story when you update versions?

[12:17] Colin O'Donnell: For alpha, we’re trying to make upgrades predictable. There’s a versioned module and upgrade notes. Day-2 ops docs cover drift and upgrades. Practically: you update module version, run plan, apply; and the installer picks up component version changes. We’ll send the upgrade/rollback policy doc too.

[12:39] Samir Khan: Rollback is important. If an upgrade breaks, can we roll back without losing logs?

[12:45] Kevin Osei: Logs are in your sink; rollback doesn’t delete them. Rollback depends on what changed — config vs images — but generally you can revert versions. We call out what’s supported in the policy.

[13:02] Priya Nair: Who has access? Do you need access to our AWS account?

[13:06] Colin O'Donnell: For private deployment, Redwood doesn’t need direct access by default. During pilot, some customers provide a break-glass role for support, but that’s optional and governed by your process. Solutions can work with you on a least-privilege support role if required.

[13:26] Elena Petrova: We will not allow persistent vendor roles. Maybe time-bound with approvals.

[13:30] Colin O'Donnell: That’s consistent with what we see.

[13:34] James Wu: Okay. Can we go deeper on the endpoint list? Like ECR, S3, CloudWatch Logs, STS… anything else like KMS?

[13:43] Bruno Silva: KMS is usually needed if you’re calling KMS API from workloads directly. For encrypt-at-rest at the AWS service level, KMS calls happen within AWS. But if your apps call KMS, then an interface endpoint may help. SSM endpoint can be required if you use SSM agent or session manager. But for Redwood Private base install, the “hard required” list is ECR API, ECR DKR, S3 gateway, STS, and DNS resolver working. CloudWatch Logs is required only if you choose that sink.

[14:19] Priya Nair: Do you need Secrets Manager endpoint?

[14:22] Bruno Silva: Only if you integrate with it for secrets retrieval. Not required for the VPC baseline module by itself.

[14:29] Kevin Osei: We’ll send a matrix that indicates “required/optional” and why.

[14:35] Samir Khan: That matrix will help a lot.

[14:38] (crosstalk) 

[14:39] Elena Petrova: Private DNS— you said private DNS enabled. We sometimes disable private DNS and manage split-horizon ourselves.

[14:47] Bruno Silva: The module has a private DNS toggle per endpoint. But we strongly recommend enabling it for endpoints like ECR and STS because otherwise you need custom resolver rules. If you want to manage split-horizon, we can support it but we’ll need to align on how the installer resolves names.

[15:09] James Wu: Yeah we run Route53 Resolver with inbound/outbound endpoints and rules. We can do it either way.

[15:16] Colin O'Donnell: We should set up a follow-up with your networking team to make sure we don’t fight your DNS setup. The installer does preflight checks like “can resolve ECR” and “can reach endpoints.”

[15:30] Priya Nair: Okay.

[15:32] Kevin Osei: Also from a security standpoint, endpoint private DNS reduces the chance of accidentally going out to public service endpoints.

[15:42] Elena Petrova: Agreed.

[15:45] Colin O'Donnell: Priya, are there any red flags so far?

[15:49] Priya Nair: Not red flags. It’s mostly “show me.” We need a security FAQ with your controls, and we need to see the defaults are actually least privilege, not marketing.

[16:01] Colin O'Donnell: Totally fair.

[16:03] Bruno Silva: We also run static checks in CI (tflint, checkov) to catch common misconfigs like public SG ingress. But of course, you’ll review the Terraform.

[16:14] James Wu: Do you ship any IAM policies as part of the module?

[16:18] Bruno Silva: Not in the baseline module itself; but the quickstart includes a “minimum apply permissions” policy for the operator. For runtime IAM, that’s cluster-level. We can share both.

[16:36] Samir Khan: For audit, do you support SSO/SAML for the console?

[16:40] Kevin Osei: Yes for the console/control plane, SSO integrations exist. In Private, it depends how you deploy the console component, but yes we support SAML/OIDC patterns. We can include that in the FAQ.

[16:56] Priya Nair: Great.

[17:00] Elena Petrova: I want to confirm the “no public egress” story. If NAT is disabled, how do you pull container images? ECR is fine via endpoint, but what about base images or OS updates?

[17:13] Bruno Silva: For Redwood images, they’re in ECR. For node OS updates, that’s up to your AMI pipeline and your patching process. If you rely on public repos, that conflicts with no-egress. Most regulated customers do a private mirror.

[17:30] James Wu: Yep.

[17:31] Priya Nair: Okay, so it’s not magic.

[17:33] Colin O'Donnell: Right. The module ensures our dependencies can be satisfied privately; it doesn’t solve all enterprise patching.

[17:42] Kevin Osei: And for any external integration like sending logs to Splunk Cloud over the internet, that’s your choice. Typically for no-egress, you’d keep logs in S3 and then ingest from your internal pipeline.

[18:00] Samir Khan: We do that.

[18:02] Colin O'Donnell: Can we shift to what you need for the next milestone? Are you aiming for an internal architecture review first or a proof-of-concept?

[18:12] Priya Nair: Internal architecture review. If that passes, we’ll do a limited POC in a non-prod AWS account but still under the same controls.

[18:21] Colin O'Donnell: Great. For that review, we’ll send:
1) Security FAQ (controls, encryption, logging)
2) Reference architecture doc (VPC topology, subnet tiers)
3) Endpoint requirements matrix
4) Example Terraform variables for the locked down topology

[18:40] James Wu: Plus any notes about STS endpoint. We’ve seen issues when vendors forget that.

[18:46] Bruno Silva: Yep, we’ll highlight STS as required.

[18:49] Elena Petrova: Also, if you have guidance on flow log fields and what to monitor, that’s helpful.

[18:55] Kevin Osei: We have a flow logs + central routing guidance doc. We’ll include that.

[19:02] Samir Khan: And we’ll need to know what logs we should retain for evidence. Like what do auditors ask.

[19:08] Kevin Osei: We can share a recommended set: installer logs during change windows, control plane audit events, and network telemetry, plus CloudTrail. But your GRC policy will drive retention.

[19:23] Priya Nair: Okay.

[19:25] Colin O'Donnell: Any other questions on competitors? I heard Bedrock come up.

[19:30] James Wu: Yeah, just context: we evaluated Bedrock and also Azure OpenAI. The problem is data residency and private network controls. Your Private approach looks better, assuming it’s supportable.

[19:44] Colin O'Donnell: That’s the goal.

[19:46] Priya Nair: Supportability is a big one. We don’t want a snowflake.

[19:49] Bruno Silva: That’s why the Terraform modules are opinionated: consistent subnetting, tagging, endpoints, and outputs for the installer. Less variance.

[20:01] Elena Petrova: Speaking of tagging, do you enforce any tags? We require owner, cost center, data classification.

[20:08] Bruno Silva: Yes, tagging schema includes env, owner, cost-center, data-class. It can be extended. We’ll share the tag list.

[20:20] Priya Nair: Great.

[20:22] (pause)

[20:24] Colin O'Donnell: I think we’ve hit the major points. Before we wrap, let’s confirm next steps.

[20:30] Colin O'Donnell: Redwood will send the Security FAQ and architecture overview doc. Kevin will include the audit/logging details. Bruno will send endpoint matrix and locked-down tfvars example. You all will confirm log sink choice and retention and any KMS constraints, and we’ll schedule a DNS/endpoints deep dive with Elena’s team.

[20:52] Priya Nair: Sounds good.

[20:54] James Wu: Works.

[20:55] Elena Petrova: Yes.

[20:56] Samir Khan: Good.

[20:58] Colin O'Donnell: Great. Thanks everyone.

[21:02] Kevin Osei: Thanks.

[21:03] Bruno Silva: Thanks.
